3.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask an elbow patient?"
- "Age, hand dominance, job and sport first."
- "Then the elbow SPINS: swelling, pain, instability, neuro symptoms, stiffness."
- "Then old injury, childhood fracture, locking and the neck."

### Pain — where is it?
| Site | Think of |
|---|---|
| Lateral | tennis elbow, radial tunnel, capitellum OCD (osteochondritis dissecans), radiocapitellar arthritis |
| Medial | golfer's elbow, cubital tunnel, MCL (medial collateral ligament) injury |
| Posterior | olecranon bursitis, posterior impingement (boxers, throwers) |
| Whole joint | osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid (RA), gout, infection, tumour |

- **Memory:** lateral = tendon, nerve or joint; medial = tendon, nerve or ligament

- Pain into the ring and little fingers → ulnar nerve at the elbow

### Other complaints
| Complaint | Points to |
|---|---|
| Locking, young patient | OCD loose body |
| Locking, older patient | loose bodies of OA |
| Giving way after a dislocation | posterolateral rotatory instability |
| Swelling with pain, female | RA — the elbow may be the first joint |
| Stiffness after injury | malunion, myositis ossificans, capsular contracture |

- Throwing athlete with medial pain → MCL insufficiency
- Childhood fracture → ask about deformity and late hand numbness

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Pain | where? Activity or night? Into the hand? |
| Function | dominant side? Work, sport, hand to mouth and head |
| Past | childhood fracture, dislocation, operations, injections |
| Neck | neck pain or arm tingling? |

- **Red flags:** hot swollen joint or bursa → infection
- **Memory:** the elbow **SPINS** — swelling, pain, instability, neuro, stiffness
- General history and opening → ch 1

3.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this elbow"
- "Standing: look front, side, behind and medial; carrying angle."
- "Sitting: feel the three points, move both elbows, test power."
- "Then special tests, nerves, pulse, neck, shoulder and wrist."

- **Whole elbow exam (video):** [▶ Faculty of Medicine, ASU e-Learning · 6:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_8tMssnZfl0)

### The route on one page
| Position | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| Standing | Look: front, side, behind, medial; carrying angle |
| Sitting | Feel: three points, radial head, soft spot, ulnar nerve, biceps |
| Sitting | Move: flexion–extension abducted; rotation, elbows at the side |
| Sitting | Measure: power of the elbow and forearm muscles |
| Sitting | Special: tennis and golfer's tests, then ligaments and instability |
| Finish | three nerves, radial pulse, neck, shoulder, wrist |

- **Memory:** Look, Feel, Move, Measure, Special; then Neuro, Vascular, Joints above/below
- Expose both arms from the shoulders down

### Look
#### Standing — four views
| View | Look for |
|---|---|
| Front, elbows extended, palms forward | carrying angle, wasting, swelling |
| Side | attitude: held flexed, hand in pocket |
| Behind | olecranon bursa, nodules, posterior scars |
| Medial | scars (ulnar nerve surgery): never forget it |

- **Attitude:** a painful elbow is held against the body
- **Memory:** at every view think **DCS** — deformity, contour and wasting, skin (Kasr Al-Ainy)

[[FIG: Fig 3.1 — Carrying angle compared and measured with a goniometer · 3.02

#### Swelling
- Effusion first fills the hollows beside the olecranon
- Then the soft spot bulges over the radiocapitellar joint

[[FIG: Fig 3.2 — Effusion fills the hollows; bursa and nodules behind · 3.02

### Feel
- Three points: olecranon tip and both epicondyles (3.3)
- Soft spot: centre of the lateral triangle — olecranon, epicondyle, radial head

[[FIG: Fig 3.3 — Lateral triangle; effusion bulges in its centre · 3.02

| Side | Feel |
|---|---|
| Lateral | supracondylar ridge, lateral epicondyle, radial head, soft spot |
| Medial | supracondylar ridge, medial epicondyle, ulnar nerve in its groove |
| Posterior | olecranon tip, olecranon fossa (elbow at 30°), triceps insertion |
| Front | biceps tendon, lacertus fibrosus, brachial artery, median nerve |

- Radial head: about 2 cm below the lateral epicondyle; turns as the forearm rotates
- Head not against the capitellum → dislocated (3.5)

[[FIG: Fig 3.4 — Radial head felt turning in pronation and supination · 3.02

- Roll the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle; thick, tender or slipping → 3.4

[[FIG: Fig 3.5 — Ulnar nerve felt in its groove · 3.02
[[FIG: Fig 3.6 — Palpating the lateral and medial epicondyles · 3.02

### Move
- Flexion–extension: arms abducted, both sides together
- Rotation: elbows at the side, flexed 90°, holding a pencil

| Movement (Nagah) | Normal |
|---|---|
| Flexion | 140° |
| Extension | 0° (to −5°) |
| Supination | 85° |
| Pronation | 75° |

- Up to 10° hyperextension is normal; more → laxity or old injury (Exam Techniques)
- Loss of full extension is the earliest sign of joint disease
- Active less than passive → tendon or nerve problem

[[FIG: Fig 3.7 — Flexion and extension compared with arms abducted · 3.02
[[FIG: Fig 3.8 — Rotation with elbows held at the sides · 3.02

### Measure — power
| Muscle | How (elbow at 90°) | Nerve |
|---|---|---|
| Biceps | resist flexion, forearm supinated | musculocutaneous |
| Brachioradialis | resist flexion, forearm neutral; muscle stands out | radial |
| Triceps | resist extension | radial |
| Pronators | resist pronation | median |
| Supinators | resist supination | radial and musculocutaneous |

- Brachioradialis recovers first after high radial palsy (Prof Mansour)

[[FIG: Fig 3.9 — Resisted elbow flexion for biceps power · 3.02

### Finish
- Ulnar, median and radial nerves → ch 5; radial pulse
- Neck, shoulder and wrist: "I would examine the cervical spine"

PITFALL — "testing rotation with the arm away from the body"
- The shoulder rotates and hides lost pronation or supination
- Say → "**I keep both elbows at the side, flexed 90°.**"

3.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you assess elbow alignment?"
- "Carrying angle in full extension, palms forward, compared with the sound side."
- "Three points: line in extension, triangle at 90° flexion."
- "Then the functional arc: 30–130° flexion, 50° each way rotation."

### Carrying angle
- **Definition:** valgus angle between arm and forearm axes, elbow extended
- Normal: men 10°, women 13° (Nagah)

[[FIG: Fig 3.10 — Carrying angle in extension; lost in flexion · 3.03

| Change | Name | Common cause |
|---|---|---|
| Increased | cubitus valgus | lateral condyle non-union; lateral physis closure |
| Decreased or reversed | cubitus varus (gunstock) | supracondylar malunion; medial physis closure |

- Varus is always abnormal
- **Memory:** **V**algus = **lateral** condyle fails; **V**arus = **supracondylar** heals badly
- Cubitus valgus stays valgus even in flexion

[[FIG: Fig 3.11 — Cubitus valgus after lateral condyle fracture; gunstock deformity · 3.03

#### Rotation deformity (Yamamoto test)
- Patient bends forward, elbow 90°, forearm behind the back
- You lift the forearm into full internal rotation
- Forearm above the horizontal → internal rotation deformity

[[FIG: Fig 3.12 — Rotation deformity: forearm angle above the back · 3.03

### Three-point relation
- Thumb on lateral epicondyle, index on olecranon, middle on medial
- Extension → straight line; 90° flexion → isosceles triangle (Exam Techniques)

| Injury | Three points |
|---|---|
| Supracondylar fracture | relation kept; triangle shifts |
| Posterior dislocation | relation lost; olecranon moves back |
| Epicondyle or intercondylar fracture | epicondyle gap changes |

- **Memory:** fracture above → triangle travels; dislocation → triangle breaks (Reider)
- Supracondylar fracture in a child: check the nerves and pulse

[[FIG: Fig 3.13 — Three points: triangle in flexion, line in extension · 3.03

### Stiff elbow
- **Functional arc:** flexion 30–130°, pronation 50°, supination 50° (Miller)
- Less → cannot reach mouth or head

| Feel at the end of passive extension | Means |
|---|---|
| Hard, bony stop | osteophyte or loose body |
| Soft, slight give | anterior capsular contracture |

- Pain on forced extension → posterior impingement
- Extension malunion: flexion stops at 90°; extension normal (Prof Mansour)

- **Memory:** lost angle in front blocks flexion; too much angle blocks extension

[[FIG: Fig 3.14 — Extension malunion: flexion stops at 90° · 3.03

PITFALL — "measuring the carrying angle in a stiff, flexed elbow"
- The angle is only true in full extension
- Say → "**The elbow does not extend, so the carrying angle cannot be judged.**"

3.03.1.b:
- **Definition:** valgus angle between arm and forearm axes, elbow extended
- Normal: men 10°, women 13° (Nagah)

|---|---|---|
| Increased | cubitus valgus | lateral condyle non-union; lateral physis closure |

3.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the elbow special tests"
- "Tender laterally → tennis tests; tender medially → golfer's test."
- "Then ligaments: valgus, varus, pivot shift; then nerve and tendon tests."

### Is it tennis elbow?
- **Memory:** **CMM** — Cozen resists, Mill stretches, Maudsley uses the middle finger

#### Cozen test
- **Aim:** lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)
- **How:** fist, pronated, radially deviated; resist wrist extension
- **Positive:** lateral epicondyle pain → tennis elbow
- **Why:** pulls the extensor origin, mainly ECRB (extensor carpi radialis brevis)
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qKSn_RNpSAE)

[[FIG: Fig 3.15 — Resisted wrist extension, thumb on the extensor origin · 3.04

#### Mill test
- **Aim:** lateral epicondylitis
- **How:** pronated, wrist flexed; slowly extend the elbow
- **Positive:** lateral epicondyle pain → tennis elbow
- **Why:** stretches the common extensor origin
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 1:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hhBIW8EDvFM)

[[FIG: Fig 3.16 — Mill test: wrist flexed, elbow extended in pronation · 3.04

#### Maudsley test
- **Aim:** lateral epicondylitis
- **How:** elbow straight, pronated; resist middle finger extension
- **Positive:** lateral epicondyle pain → tennis elbow (Nagah)
- **Why:** loads the ECRB and extensor digitorum origin
- **Trap:** radial tunnel also hurts; tenderness site decides (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BaxgmHT_2eQ)

[[FIG: Fig 3.17 — Resisted middle finger extension · 3.04

### Is it golfer's elbow?
#### Golfer's elbow test
- **Aim:** medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)
- **How:** patient flexes the wrist; you try to straighten it
- **Positive:** pain at the medial epicondyle → golfer's elbow
- **Why:** loads the common flexor–pronator origin
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vc367Nl7aAc)

[[FIG: Fig 3.18 — Passive stretch and resisted wrist flexion · 3.04

### Is the medial ligament torn?
- **Memory:** unlock the olecranon first — always test in slight flexion

#### Valgus stress test (elbow)
- **Aim:** MCL (ulnar collateral ligament) tear
- **How:** shoulder in ER, elbow about 30°; push into valgus
- **Positive:** medial opening or pain → MCL injury
- **Why:** 30° unlocks the olecranon from its fossa
- **Trap:** pronate: supination also opens with LUCL laxity (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xF9_5fbJ8A)

[[FIG: Fig 3.19 — Valgus stress, humerus externally rotated · 3.04

#### Moving valgus stress test
- **Aim:** MCL tear in the throwing athlete
- **How:** shoulder 90° abducted, in ER; hold valgus, extend quickly
- **Positive:** medial pain between 120° and 70° → MCL tear
- **Why:** valgus through the arc; most accurate MCL test (Campbell)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 2:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JIU_kv5VoQk)

[[FIG: Fig 3.20 — Moving valgus: valgus held while the elbow extends · 3.04

#### Milking manoeuvre
- **Aim:** partial MCL tear
- **How:** elbow about 70°, supinated; pull the thumb down
- **Positive:** apprehension, pain or opening → MCL injury
- **Why:** thumb pull = valgus on the flexed elbow
- **Video:** [▶ Sports Med Review · 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2C1h0G3VfEU)

[[FIG: Fig 3.21 — Milking: thumb pulled, medial joint felt · 3.04

### Is the lateral ligament torn?
#### Varus stress test (elbow)
- **Aim:** LCL (lateral collateral ligament) tear
- **How:** shoulder in full IR, elbow about 30°; push into varus
- **Positive:** lateral opening → LCL injury
- **Why:** IR locks the shoulder; force reaches the elbow
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5zl8GsG3hR4)

[[FIG: Fig 3.22 — Varus stress, humerus internally rotated · 3.04

### Is there posterolateral rotatory instability?
- PLRI = posterolateral rotatory instability; LUCL = lateral ulnar collateral ligament
- **Memory:** the injury position = **supination + valgus + axial load**

#### Lateral pivot shift test
- **Aim:** PLRI from LUCL insufficiency
- **How:** supine, arm overhead, supinated; valgus, axial load, then flex
- **Positive:** dimple, then a clunk near 40° flexion → PLRI
- **Why:** flexion tightens the triceps and reduces the joint
- **Trap:** awake → apprehension only; clunk needs anaesthesia (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 1:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N1mObCAcKDg)

[[FIG: Fig 3.23 — Pivot shift: subluxed in extension, reduced on flexion · 3.04

#### Chair push-up test
- **Aim:** PLRI — apprehension test
- **How:** patient pushes up from a chair, forearms supinated
- **Positive:** apprehension; will not fully extend → PLRI
- **Why:** same axial load, valgus and supination as the injury
- **Video:** [▶ CCEDseminars · 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cldmIKCYbuI)

[[FIG: Fig 3.24 — Rising from a chair, forearms supinated; floor push-up · 3.04

#### Table-top relocation test
- **Aim:** PLRI — confirm the apprehension
- **How:** push-up on a table edge; repeat, thumb on the radial head
- **Positive:** apprehension gone with thumb support → PLRI (Nagah)
- **Why:** thumb stops the radial head slipping back
- **Video:** [▶ CCEDseminars · 1:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cleWpZGL-CA)

[[FIG: Fig 3.25 — Thumb supports the radial head during the push-up · 3.04

### Is the ulnar nerve irritated?
- Cubital tunnel syndrome detail and the hand signs → ch 5

#### Tinel sign (cubital tunnel)
- **Aim:** ulnar nerve irritation at the elbow
- **How:** tap the nerve between olecranon and medial epicondyle
- **Positive:** ring and little finger tingling → ulnar irritation
- **Why:** an irritated nerve fires when tapped
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbiPcPqRiy4)

[[FIG: Fig 3.26 — Tapping the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel · 3.04

- Elbow flexion test → ch 5 (5.4): ring and little tingling in 1 minute

#### Ulnar nerve subluxation test
- **Aim:** unstable (subluxing) ulnar nerve
- **How:** finger in the groove; flex and extend the elbow
- **Positive:** nerve snaps over the epicondyle in flexion → subluxing
- **Why:** up to 10% of people have a mobile nerve (Exam Techniques)
- **Video:** [▶ Nick Ferran (Shoulder & Elbow London) · 2:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VqlIfc1Smn4)

[[FIG: Fig 3.27 — Nerve felt slipping forward over the epicondyle · 3.04

### Is a tendon torn?
#### Hook test
- **Aim:** complete distal biceps tendon rupture
- **How:** elbow 90°, supinated; hook the index under the tendon from lateral
- **Positive:** no cord to hook → complete rupture
- **Why:** sensitivity near 100% (Prof Mansour)
- **Trap:** partial tear or intact lacertus fibrosus feels like a tendon
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7fcDs0H3-xo)

[[FIG: Fig 3.28 — Reverse Popeye, bruising, and the hook test · 3.04

#### Triceps resisted extension
- **Aim:** triceps tendon tear
- **How:** elbow flexed; you resist extension
- **Positive:** pain → partial; cannot extend against gravity → avulsion
- **Why:** triceps = the main elbow extender
- **Video:** [▶ Ball State Athletic Training · 0:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YEAYCNICfss)

[[FIG: Fig 3.29 — Resisted elbow extension for triceps · 3.04

### Is the radiocapitellar joint damaged?
#### Radiocapitellar compression test
- **Aim:** radiocapitellar cartilage damage, capitellum OCD
- **How:** valgus and axial load on the joint while rotating
- **Positive:** pain or crepitus → chondromalacia (Campbell)
- **Why:** rotation grinds the radial head on the capitellum
- **Video:** [▶ Perspectives RMT · 0:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i1KQgagP4CU)

[[FIG: Fig 3.30 — Thumb on the radiocapitellar joint during rotation · 3.04

### Other tests
| Test | Point |
|---|---|
| Chair lift test | lift a chair, elbows straight → tennis elbow |
| Posterolateral drawer | proximal forearm pushed posterolaterally → PLRI |
| Biceps squeeze | elbow 60–80°, squeeze biceps → no supination = rupture |
| Posterior / anterior impingement | snap into full extension / flexion → pain |
| Radial tunnel tests | resisted supination → radial neck pain |

[[FIG: Fig 3.31 — Chair lift and Thomsen tests for tennis elbow · 3.04

PITFALL — "calling every lateral pain tennis elbow"
- Radial tunnel pain: distal, over the radial neck, wakes at night (Prof Mansour)
- Say → "**Tenderness is at the epicondyle, not distal; this is tennis elbow.**"

3.04.2.b:
#### Golfer's elbow test
- **Aim:** medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)
- **How:** patient flexes the wrist; you try to straighten it
- **Positive:** pain at the medial epicondyle → golfer's elbow
- **Why:** loads the common flexor–pronator origin
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vc367Nl7aAc)

[[FIG: Fig 3.18 — Passive stretch and resisted wrist flexion · 3.04

3.04.3.b:
- **Memory:** unlock the olecranon first — always test in slight flexion

#### Valgus stress test (elbow)
- **Aim:** MCL (ulnar collateral ligament) tear
- **How:** shoulder in ER, elbow about 30°; push into valgus
- **Positive:** medial opening or pain → MCL injury
- **Why:** 30° unlocks the olecranon from its fossa
- **Trap:** pronate: supination also opens with LUCL laxity (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xF9_5fbJ8A)

[[FIG: Fig 3.19 — Valgus stress, humerus externally rotated · 3.04

#### Moving valgus stress test
- **Aim:** MCL tear in the throwing athlete
- **How:** shoulder 90° abducted, in ER; hold valgus, extend quickly
- **Positive:** medial pain between 120° and 70° → MCL tear
- **Why:** valgus through the arc; most accurate MCL test (Campbell)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 2:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JIU_kv5VoQk)

[[FIG: Fig 3.20 — Moving valgus: valgus held while the elbow extends · 3.04

#### Milking manoeuvre
- **Aim:** partial MCL tear
- **How:** elbow about 70°, supinated; pull the thumb down
- **Positive:** apprehension, pain or opening → MCL injury
- **Why:** thumb pull = valgus on the flexed elbow
- **Video:** [▶ Sports Med Review · 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2C1h0G3VfEU)

[[FIG: Fig 3.21 — Milking: thumb pulled, medial joint felt · 3.04

3.04.4.b:
#### Varus stress test (elbow)
- **Aim:** LCL (lateral collateral ligament) tear
- **How:** shoulder in full IR, elbow about 30°; push into varus
- **Positive:** lateral opening → LCL injury
- **Why:** IR locks the shoulder; force reaches the elbow
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5zl8GsG3hR4)

[[FIG: Fig 3.22 — Varus stress, humerus internally rotated · 3.04

3.04.5.b:
- PLRI = posterolateral rotatory instability; LUCL = lateral ulnar collateral ligament
- **Memory:** the injury position = **supination + valgus + axial load**

#### Lateral pivot shift test
- **Aim:** PLRI from LUCL insufficiency
- **How:** supine, arm overhead, supinated; valgus, axial load, then flex
- **Positive:** dimple, then a clunk near 40° flexion → PLRI
- **Why:** flexion tightens the triceps and reduces the joint
- **Trap:** awake → apprehension only; clunk needs anaesthesia (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 1:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N1mObCAcKDg)

[[FIG: Fig 3.23 — Pivot shift: subluxed in extension, reduced on flexion · 3.04

#### Chair push-up test
- **Aim:** PLRI — apprehension test
- **How:** patient pushes up from a chair, forearms supinated
- **Positive:** apprehension; will not fully extend → PLRI
- **Why:** same axial load, valgus and supination as the injury
- **Video:** [▶ CCEDseminars · 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cldmIKCYbuI)

[[FIG: Fig 3.24 — Rising from a chair, forearms supinated; floor push-up · 3.04

#### Table-top relocation test
- **Aim:** PLRI — confirm the apprehension
- **How:** push-up on a table edge; repeat, thumb on the radial head
- **Positive:** apprehension gone with thumb support → PLRI (Nagah)
- **Why:** thumb stops the radial head slipping back
- **Video:** [▶ CCEDseminars · 1:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cleWpZGL-CA)

[[FIG: Fig 3.25 — Thumb supports the radial head during the push-up · 3.04

3.04.6.b:
- Cubital tunnel syndrome detail and the hand signs → ch 5

#### Tinel sign (cubital tunnel)
- **Aim:** ulnar nerve irritation at the elbow
- **How:** tap the nerve between olecranon and medial epicondyle
- **Positive:** ring and little finger tingling → ulnar irritation
- **Why:** an irritated nerve fires when tapped
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbiPcPqRiy4)

[[FIG: Fig 3.26 — Tapping the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel · 3.04

- Elbow flexion test → ch 5 (5.4): ring and little tingling in 1 minute

#### Ulnar nerve subluxation test
- **Aim:** unstable (subluxing) ulnar nerve
- **How:** finger in the groove; flex and extend the elbow
- **Positive:** nerve snaps over the epicondyle in flexion → subluxing
- **Why:** up to 10% of people have a mobile nerve (Exam Techniques)
- **Video:** [▶ Nick Ferran (Shoulder & Elbow London) · 2:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VqlIfc1Smn4)

[[FIG: Fig 3.27 — Nerve felt slipping forward over the epicondyle · 3.04

3.04.7.b:
#### Hook test
- **Aim:** complete distal biceps tendon rupture
- **How:** elbow 90°, supinated; hook the index under the tendon from lateral
- **Positive:** no cord to hook → complete rupture
- **Why:** sensitivity near 100% (Prof Mansour)
- **Trap:** partial tear or intact lacertus fibrosus feels like a tendon
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7fcDs0H3-xo)

[[FIG: Fig 3.28 — Reverse Popeye, bruising, and the hook test · 3.04

#### Triceps resisted extension
- **Aim:** triceps tendon tear
- **How:** elbow flexed; you resist extension
- **Positive:** pain → partial; cannot extend against gravity → avulsion
- **Why:** triceps = the main elbow extender
- **Video:** [▶ Ball State Athletic Training · 0:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YEAYCNICfss)

[[FIG: Fig 3.29 — Resisted elbow extension for triceps · 3.04

3.04.8.b:
#### Radiocapitellar compression test
- **Aim:** radiocapitellar cartilage damage, capitellum OCD
- **How:** valgus and axial load on the joint while rotating
- **Positive:** pain or crepitus → chondromalacia (Campbell)
- **Why:** rotation grinds the radial head on the capitellum
- **Video:** [▶ Perspectives RMT · 0:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i1KQgagP4CU)

[[FIG: Fig 3.30 — Thumb on the radiocapitellar joint during rotation · 3.04

3.04.9.b:
| Test | Point |
|---|---|
| Chair lift test | lift a chair, elbows straight → tennis elbow |
| Posterolateral drawer | proximal forearm pushed posterolaterally → PLRI |
| Biceps squeeze | elbow 60–80°, squeeze biceps → no supination = rupture |
| Posterior / anterior impingement | snap into full extension / flexion → pain |
| Radial tunnel tests | resisted supination → radial neck pain |

[[FIG: Fig 3.31 — Chair lift and Thomsen tests for tennis elbow · 3.04

PITFALL — "calling every lateral pain tennis elbow"
- Radial tunnel pain: distal, over the radial neck, wakes at night (Prof Mansour)
- Say → "**Tenderness is at the epicondyle, not distal; this is tennis elbow.**"

3.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "two-minute elbow short case"
- "Spot: carrying angle, scar, swelling, attitude. Do: three points, range, ulnar nerve."
- "Say: one diagnosis and one differential."

### Cubitus varus (gunstock deformity)
- **Spot:** forearm angled in; old supracondylar fracture in childhood
- **Do:** three points kept; range near normal; Yamamoto test
- **Say:** "Cubitus varus after supracondylar malunion. Differential: medial physeal arrest."

- Mostly cosmetic; late PLRI and ulnar nerve symptoms may follow
- Pure supracondylar fracture → varus does not recur after correction (Nagah)

[[FIG: Fig 3.32 — Gunstock deformity; course case of a varus left elbow · 3.05

### Cubitus valgus with tardy ulnar palsy
- **Spot:** forearm angled out; first web wasting, ulnar claw
- **Do:** Tinel and flexion test; ulnar nerve exam → ch 5
- **Say:** "Cubitus valgus, tardy ulnar palsy. Differential: old Monteggia."

- Palsy appears slowly, often between 30 and 50 years (McRae)

[[FIG: Fig 3.33 — Cubitus valgus and the ulnar claw hand · 3.05

### Stiff elbow
- **Spot:** held flexed, old scar, hand-to-mouth hard
- **Do:** arc of flexion and rotation; end feel; ulnar nerve
- **Say:** "Post-traumatic stiff elbow, arc 40–100°. Differential: heterotopic ossification."

- Myositis ossificans after dislocation → hard block to flexion

[[FIG: Fig 3.34 — Myositis ossificans and a loose body · 3.05

### Tennis elbow
- **Spot:** middle-aged worker; no swelling, no deformity
- **Do:** tender just distal to the lateral epicondyle; Cozen, Mill
- **Say:** "Right lateral epicondylitis. Differential: radial tunnel syndrome."

- Commonest elbow pain in clinic, age 35–50 (McRae)

[[FIG: Fig 3.35 — Point tenderness at the extensor origin · 3.05

### Recurrent posterolateral instability
- **Spot:** young adult, old dislocation, "the elbow slips"
- **Do:** chair push-up, table-top relocation
- **Say:** "Left PLRI from LUCL insufficiency. Differential: radial head instability."

- Dislocation tears from lateral to medial: LUCL → capsule → MCL (Nagah)
- LCL-deficient elbow is more stable in pronation

[[FIG: Fig 3.36 — Horii circle: injury travels lateral to medial · 3.05

### Olecranon bursitis
- **Spot:** soft swelling behind the olecranon
- **Do:** fluctuant; feel warmth and redness; look for nodules
- **Say:** "Olecranon bursitis, likely septic. Differential: rheumatoid nodule."

- Hot red skin → infection; slightly warm → sterile bursitis

[[FIG: Fig 3.37 — Olecranon bursitis · 3.05

### Dislocated radial head (congenital or missed Monteggia)
- **Spot:** lateral or front lump; rotation lost
- **Do:** head off the capitellum; check the posterior interosseous nerve
- **Say:** "Missed Monteggia, radial head dislocated. Differential: congenital dislocation."

- Congenital: often bilateral, painless, convex head, no injury (Miller)
- Child's ulnar bow can hide a Monteggia; check the proximal radioulnar joint (Prof Mansour)

[[FIG: Fig 3.38 — Radiocapitellar line; congenital and missed Monteggia · 3.05

PITFALL — "fixing the varus but forgetting the nerve"
- Varus and valgus can both stretch the ulnar nerve
- Say → "**I would examine the ulnar nerve before planning an osteotomy.**"

3.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "present your case"
- "Who, dominant side, what happened; look, feel, move; then my diagnosis."
- "Name the deformity, the range, and the nerve status in every elbow."

### Present it like this
| Part | Say |
|---|---|
| History | "A 20-year-old right-handed student; left supracondylar fracture at 6." |
| Look | "Left cubitus varus about 15°; no scars." |
| Feel | "Three-point relation normal; ulnar nerve not tender." |
| Move | "Flexion 0–130°; full rotation; Yamamoto test shows internal rotation." |
| Verdict | "Cubitus varus from supracondylar malunion; nerves intact; I would image." |

### Differential of a painful stiff elbow
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Traumatic | malunion, myositis ossificans, capsular contracture |
| Inflammatory | RA, gout, infection, tuberculosis |
| Neoplastic | synovial chondromatosis, tumour |
| Degenerative | primary OA in manual workers, OA after OCD |
| Referred | cervical spine |

- **Memory:** TIN-DR — traumatic, inflammatory, neoplastic, degenerative, referred

### The Examiner Asks
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Normal carrying angle? | men 10°, women 13° |
| Commonest cause of cubitus varus? | supracondylar fracture malunion |
| Cause of cubitus valgus? | lateral condyle non-union |
| Three points in a supracondylar fracture? | relation kept |
| Why test ligaments at 30°? | unlocks the olecranon from its fossa |
| Functional arc? | 30–130° flexion, 50° each rotation |
| Pivot shift position? | supination, valgus, axial load |
| First muscle to recover in radial palsy? | brachioradialis |
| Hook from which side? | lateral, to avoid the lacertus |
| Why elbows at the side for rotation? | stops shoulder rotation |
| Tardy ulnar palsy follows? | cubitus valgus |
| Congenital vs traumatic radial head? | congenital: convex head, often bilateral |
